title: TB5-02831
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has not submitted new evidence in support of his appeal. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own determination that he is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Determination

This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to Section 111(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter to the Refugee Protection Division for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. Background

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he is a Shia Muslim. He worked for his stepfather in Pakistan, who is a Sunni Muslim. He stated that on XXXX XXXX, 2010 he was at a Shia procession when Sunni extremists staged three suicide attacks in the middle of the congregation. He alleged that on XXXX XXXX, 2012, while in Gujarat, he was at the XXXX XXXX when extremists tried to stop the peaceful gathering outside. He tried to defuse the situation and was beaten. He was saved by the XXXX XXXX security. He filed a complaint at the police station and was advised to stay away from his religious activities.

He began to arrange gatherings among Shia scholars, professors and prominent figures from his community. He was quite vocal at these gatherings. On XXXX XXXX, 2013 he was in XXXX for a week on business. He was a part of a procession when extremists began throwing rocks and shooting from the rooftop of the mosque. The claimant was identified and beaten by them. He was taken to a local clinic and treated. On XXXX XXXX, 2014 he hosted a meeting at his house of prominent Shia community figures. The agenda of the meeting was to form a NGO. A couple of days later, people from the Sunni extremist group, Lashkare-e-jhangvi, came to his home and threatened his wife and children telling them that the claimant should stop his religious activities or he would face the consequences and be killed. He reported the incident to the XXXX XXXX, who advised him to go to the police station to file a complaint and get police protection. The police advised him that these people were too dangerous and politically powerful and that they could track anybody. They advised him that it was best to leave his house and hide from them as this was happening to people all over the country.

The following night he received a threatening telephone call from the extremists. The same night gunshots were fired in front of the main gate of his home and a bullet shattered the rear glass of his car. He went to the XXXX XXXX the next day and told them about the threat and was advised that another member of that XXXX XXXX had been killed after receiving similar kinds of threats a little while ago. They advised him to leave his home immediately and if possible leave the country as well. The claimant's stepfather helped him to get a Canadian visa and he left Pakistan to save his life.
The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard on January 13, 2015. In a decision of February 26, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim finding the Appellant was not credible.

The RPD found: a) The Appellant was not credible and lacked subjective fear in respect of his delay in departing Pakistan and the delay in making a claim upon arrival in Canada. b) The Appellant's activities in organizing a luncheon to establish an NGO were not credible. c) The threats from Sipah-E-Sahaba (SSP) were not credible d) The Appellant had a viable internal flight alternative (IFA)

The Appellant submits: 1. The RPD made unsustainable credibility findings in reference to the: * Delay in claiming protection in Canada * Delay in leaving Pakistan * Appellant's time in hiding * Appellant's membership in the XXXX XXXX * threats by the Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and the SSP. 2. The RPD erred by failing to address or consider critical documentary evidence that corroborates the Appellant's core allegations and contradicts the RPD's credibility findings.

Counsel has made submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of a RPD decision. However, the RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

While there has been some conflict in the case law from the Federal Court regarding the standard of review to be applied by the RAD when reviewing RPD decisions, Justice Martineau in Alyafi2 has said that, in the face of this conflict, the Federal Court should allow the RAD to apply either approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decisions has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada.

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person is need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions.
The RPD found that the determinative issue in this claim was credibility and the availability of an IFA in Islamabad. Corroborating Documentary Evidence Unsustainable Credibility Findings
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The RPD found the Appellant was not credible in areas associated with his delay in leaving Pakistan, his hosting of a luncheon at his home and threats received from Lashkare-e-jhangvi and Sipah-E-Sahaba. The Appellant submits the RPD erred by failing to address or consider critical documentary evidence that corroborates the Appellant's core allegations and contradicts the RPD's credibility findings. The Appellant argues that this constitutes a reviewable error.
The RAD finds the Appellant's argument has merit.

The Appellant identified seven documents that corroborate the Appellant's core allegations: * A letter from the editor of the magazine where the Appellant worked, confirming that he was targeted and denied protection by the police.3 * A letter from the Appellant's Iman, confirming events involving extremists on XXXX XXXX, 2012.4 * A medical report corroborating the Appellant's injuries on XXXX XXXX, 2012.5 * A letter from the XXXX confirming they urged the Appellant to flee Pakistan.6 * A medical report corroborating injuries in an incident in XXXX 2012.7 * A police report concerning the events of XXXX XXXX, 20148 * A court order ordering the XXXX police to provide protection to the Appellant and his wife. 9

In particular the Appellant submits that the RPD during the hearing expressed reliability concerns with the court order10 submitted by the Appellant concerning his step-father approaching the court in XXXX, Pakistan and seeking police protection for the threats against the Appellant. The Appellant notes that the RPD considered this document so important to the claim that it was decided the court order would be sent to Pakistan for verification. The Appellant argues that the RPD did not address the AIF findings in its Reasons, nor did it address any findings associated with this document.

The RAD has reviewed the audio recording of the hearing, which confirms the RPD held a mid-hearing conference with the Appellant's counsel and identified that there were concerns with the documents. The RPD on the record explained that it was going to initiate an Access to Information Form request (AIF) to ascertain the provenance of the court documents. The RPD subsequently explained the process to the Appellant, prepared the required forms and obtained the Appellant's signature to initiate the inquiry. The RPD continued the hearing and sought submissions from Appellant's counsel aside from the documents sent for the AIF. The RPD explained on the record that it anticipated receiving the AIF in approximately one month. The RPD further noted upon receipt of the AIF results it would contact Appellant's counsel and seek submissions on the finding. The RPD then noted that it would then decide on whether additional action was needed. The RPD also explained that if the AIF results were not received in a timely manner that it would assess what further action was to be taken. The hearing was then adjourned waiting for receipt of the AIF documents.

The RAD examined the record and finds no additional information was communicated to the Appellant or his counsel. The RAD finds the RPD had a duty to communicate information to the Appellant and his counsel and seek submissions in respect to the AIF request or any decision made in respect of choosing to render a decision in the absence of the AIF. The RAD finds the RPD has violated the principles of natural justice by making its determination without considering the submissions of Appellant's counsel or at the very least explaining why it chose to dispense with the AIF request and how it assessed the document in rendering its decision.

The RAD notes in its review of the audio recording of the hearing that the RPD did address a number of the documents listed above by the Appellant in its questioning. The RAD having reviewed the RPD Reasons finds the RPD has arrived at credibility conclusions in its decision through selectively utilizing supporting documents. The RAD further finds that the RPD did not address whether it found the Appellant's additional supporting documents credible and/or probative in reference to the basis of his claim for refugee protection.

The RAD has considered the statements of the Federal Court in Karim v Canada:11 More importantly, however, I find that the Board erred in failing to refer to evidence that corroborated the Applicant's testimony but contradicted the Board's findings. It is not necessary for the Board to refer to every document in the decision, since there is a presumption that the Board has considered all the evidence: see Hassan v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1992), 147 NR 317, at para 3 (FCA); Lewis v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1195, at para 19. However, the more important or relevant the evidence is to a central issue, the more likely a Court will infer from the Board's silence that the evidence was ignored: Cepeda-Gutierrez v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1998), 157 FTR 35, at paras 15-17 (FCTD). In particular, where the Board fails to refer to evidence that contradicts its conclusion, it may be easier to infer that the Board overlooked this evidence. Moreover, it is an error to say there is "no evidence" of an allegation when there is in fact some evidence: Abdi v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1993), 68 FTR 319 (FCTD).

The RAD finds that it was necessary for the RPD to provide a rationale for why it chose not to assess documents, which address issues that are central to the claim, prior to making determinative credibility findings that are fatal to the claim. The RPD subsequently utilized aspects of the credibility findings to ground its internal flight alternative findings. In failing to address the Appellant's applicable personal documentary evidence in its reasons, and how this evidence undermines or, why it preferred some documentary evidence over other evidence, the RPD has failed to demonstrate that it has fairly assessed the evidence in the record. In addition the RPD's application of the unsustainable credibility findings to the Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) finding, renders the IFA finding unsustainable.
The RAD finds that the RPD's credibility findings in this regard cannot be sustained.
Accordingly, the RAD finds the RPD decision must be set aside. Disposition and Remedy

Section 111(1) of IRPA allows the RAD to: (a) confirm the determination of the Refugee Protection Division; (b) set aside a decision of the RPD and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made; (c) refer the matter back to the RPD, giving the directions to the RPD that it considers appropriate.

The RAD can only make the referral described in 111(1)(c) if it was of the opinion that the decision of the RPD was wrong in law, in fact, or in mixed law and fact, and if the RAD cannot make a decision to confirm or substitute the RPD's decision without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD.12

The Appellant asks the RAD to substitute its own determination that he is a Convention refugee. The RAD is not in a position to do so. There remain significant outstanding issues, which the RAD is not able to address without rehearing the evidence. These issues were not appropriately addressed by the RPD, and the RAD is therefore not able to substitute its own determination.

In particular, the RAD notes the following concerns: * If the RPD finds the court documents to be genuine, does this impact a component of state protection? For example: Does it place an onus on the Appellant to approach higher authorities if they fail to provide protection? * The IFA assessment did not sufficiently explore the Appellant's ability to relocate to the proposed IFA location.

The RAD has not seen or questioned the Appellant and is therefore in no position to make its own credibility finding on his refugee claim. For these reasons, the RAD cannot substitute its own determination for that of the RPD, and it cannot find the Appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

Pursuant to Section 111(c) of IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the Refugee Protection Division for re-determination by a differently constituted panel. This appeal is allowed.
